h1:
Khanom Jeen in Sisaket
A Curry-Broth Breakfast with Piles of Fresh Greens
intro: For a lot of people in Sisaket, breakfast starts with a bowl of khanom jeen — soft rice noodles drowned in hot curry broth, then a heap of fresh greens piled on top until the plate overflows. Some shops do an Isan-style fish broth, others go for a rich Pradok-style curry broth that drifted in from Korat. We went around looking for the places that are actually open right now and sorted them by area, price and opening hours, in case you pass through Sisaket and want to land at the right shop.

blocks.html: Khanom jeen in Sisaket isn't just one thing. Go shop to shop and you'll find Isan fish broth with a fragrant hit of pla ra (fermented fish), a creamier coconut-milk broth, and the rich curry broth people casually call Pradok style — which is really a famous recipe from Ban Pradok in Korat that spread through the lower Isan region until it became a familiar taste around here. What every shop shares is the fresh greens: Sisaket is shallot-and-garlic country, so local vegetables show up in a full plate at nearly every spot.

blocks.text: How Pradok khanom jeen and curry broth differ from fish broth

blocks.html: Pradok-style curry broth comes from pounding a fresh curry paste — fingerroot, shallot, garlic, chili — then stirring finely pounded fish into the broth. Some versions are thin and a touch spicy, others add coconut milk to soften it. The difference from Isan pla ra broth is that fermented fish isn't the star, so the smell is milder, kids can eat it, and people who skip pla ra are fine with it. Nam ya pa, on the other hand, uses more spices and wild greens and runs hotter. Pick whichever you like, shop by shop.

items: Curry broth (Pradok style) — freshly pounded curry paste, smooth fish, mild aroma, easy for kids
Isan fish broth — made with pla ra or boiled fish, stronger smell, a bold homestyle taste
Coconut-milk broth — coconut milk added, thicker and softer, sweeter and richer, good if you don't want much heat
Chili dip / green curry — some shops offer these as an extra topping option

blocks.text: The Sisaket khanom jeen shops locals really go to

blocks.html: Picked from real reviews and shops still open at the moment. The order isn't a fixed ranking of who's better — it follows how easy they are to reach, whether they genuinely open for breakfast, and how much people talk about them. Prices are rough ranges and can shift day to day, so call to check hours before you head out if it's a long drive.

items.name: Sisaket Khanom Jeen
items.blurb: The shop people mention most when they search for khanom jeen in town. Reviews praise the generous toppings and the plate piled high with fresh greens. There are several broths to choose from, including fish broth. Opens early, and you can order delivery via LINE MAN if you'd rather not sit in.
items.meta: In Sisaket town · breakfast to mid-morning

items.name: Yai Lit Khanom Jeen Buffet
items.blurb: If you eat a lot, try this — an all-you-can-eat buffet at a single price. You can pick from several broths, and the fresh greens are laid out in piles to help yourself. Great for coming with a group and settling in for a long morning meal.

items.name: Pa Kaew Khanom Jeen Mor Din
items.blurb: The draw here is keeping the broth in a clay pot, which keeps it pleasantly warm with a homey aroma. The flavor leans traditional, and people in the area drop by for breakfast regularly.

items.name: Khun Yai Khanom Jeen, Sisaket
items.blurb: Next to Makro Sisaket, on the left at the entrance to the Karnkeha housing estate — easy to find if you're driving. The curry broth is rich and they're generous with the fresh greens. Good for a stop before heading into town.

items.name: Khanom Jeen Buffet 59 (PTT Pho / Phanta Market branches)
items.blurb: Another buffet Sisaket locals talk about, with two branches. One sits inside the PTT Pho gas station, an easy stop on the road. Several broths and fresh greens to choose from, and you can help yourself freely.

items.name: Khanom Jeen Buffet, PTT Ban Non Dang
items.blurb: A khanom jeen buffet inside the PTT gas station at Ban Non Dang, Mueang district. Good for drivers passing by who want a quick breakfast — a big pile of greens to serve yourself and several broths.

items.name: Tha Ruea Khanom Jeen (Yai Wan, the old shop)
items.blurb: A long-running shop in the Tha Ruea area, well known to longtime locals. Same old hands at the wok, a homey broth — nothing flashy, but it fills you up and warms you over. Good for anyone who likes an old-school shop atmosphere.

items.name: Khanom Jeen, Sisaket Shopping Center Market
items.blurb: A longtime shop in the Shopping Center market downtown. Plenty of people have eaten here since they were kids. Opens early, perfect for grabbing a bowl while you do your market shopping. Easy on the wallet, with several broths to choose from.

blocks.title: Make it taste better
blocks.html: Khanom jeen nam ya is best while the broth is still hot, so the noodles don't clump. Pile on a mix of fresh greens — long beans, lemon basil, pickled mustard — then squeeze in a little lime with some chili flakes, and the flavor rounds out a lot. Most buffets taste best in the morning because the broth is freshly made; go too late and the greens may start running out.

blocks.text: When to go and how to prepare

items: Morning is prime time — most khanom jeen shops in Sisaket sell from early to noon, and some sell out earlier. If you want a popular shop, getting there before 10 a.m. is the safe bet.
Carry cash — market shops and old-school spots still mostly take cash. Some have PromptPay, but not all.
Buffets are best for groups — Yai Lit, Buffet 59 and the gas-station shops are great for a group; you can eat your fill and it works out better value than ordering by the plate.
Leave time for travel — some shops are out of town or in roadside gas stations, so check the location on a map first so you don't get lost.

blocks.text: Pair it with other eats in town

blocks.html: If you're still hungry after the khanom jeen, Sisaket has plenty more breakfast and street food to keep going — rice-noodle soup, old-style coffee, and local sweets. Plan a morning eating circuit and you can hit several shops in one trip.

items.name: Isan Food in Sisaket
items.blurb: Som tam, larb, koi and other bold local dishes that pair easily with khanom jeen.

faq.q: What is Pradok khanom jeen, and what's its connection to Sisaket?
faq.a: Pradok khanom jeen is a well-known curry-broth recipe from Ban Pradok in Nakhon Ratchasima province, built on freshly pounded curry paste and smooth fish, with only a mild pla ra smell. The recipe spread through the lower Isan region, including Sisaket, until many shops made it and the name stuck — though it doesn't mean every shop in Sisaket follows the Pradok recipe.

faq.q: Where can I eat Sisaket khanom jeen for breakfast?
faq.a: The shops people mention most are Sisaket Khanom Jeen in town, Pa Kaew Khanom Jeen Mor Din, the Khun Yai shop next to Makro, and the shop in the Shopping Center market. Most open from early morning to noon — best to go before 10 a.m. since some sell out fast.

faq.q: Are there khanom jeen buffets in Sisaket, and how much do they cost?
faq.a: There are several, such as Yai Lit Khanom Jeen Buffet at around 49 THB per person, and Khanom Jeen Buffet 59 with branches at the PTT Pho gas station and Phanta Market. You can help yourself to broth and fresh greens all you like — great for coming with a group.

faq.q: What's the difference between curry broth and fish broth?
faq.a: Curry broth leans on freshly pounded curry paste and smooth fish, with a milder smell that's easy for kids. Isan fish broth usually uses pla ra or boiled fish, with a stronger smell and bolder taste. Pick whichever you prefer — many shops offer both.

faq.q: Do I need to bring cash?
faq.a: Carrying some cash is recommended, since market shops and old-school spots still mostly take cash. Some have PromptPay, but not every shop.
